[MUQATIL:4:23/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The listed mothers, daughters, sisters, aunts, and nieces are forbidden through blood relationship.
[MUQATIL:4:23/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Foster mothers and sisters, mothers-in-law, and stepdaughters of wives with whom the man has consummated marriage are forbidden.
[MUQATIL:4:23/r3] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | If he has not consummated marriage with their mothers, there is no sin in marrying the daughters.
[MUQATIL:4:23/r4] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | A son's wife is forbidden when the son is the man's biological child, born from his loins rather than adopted; this is affinity.
[MUQATIL:4:23/r5] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Combining two sisters is forbidden, except when one is held in ownership and he marries her to someone else.
[MUQATIL:4:23/r6] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The exception for past conduct means God forgives intercourse with two sisters before the prohibition.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايحركفيهالتنوينفيالأسماءالغالبة)#639/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Tanwin is normally retained before a descriptive or annexed second name; it is omitted only when the combination has become a dominant identifying name such as ابن الزبير.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايحركفيهالتنوينفيالأسماءالغالبة)#639/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil keeps tanwin in زيد ابن زيدك: Zayd is made definite by the attached pronoun, not by becoming a dominant compound name; Yunus omits tanwin.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايحركفيهالتنوينفيالأسماءالغالبة)#639/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · يونس | reports | Yunus does not pronounce tanwin in زيد ابن زيدك, differing from al-Khalil's preferred analogical analysis.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايحركفيهالتنوينفيالأسماءالغالبة)#639/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | If ابن is an apposition or repetition rather than an adjective, tanwin remains; an ordinary name like أخو زيد also keeps tanwin before ابن عمرو.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايحركفيهالتنوينفيالأسماءالغالبة)#639/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The form بني عمرو is attributed to Abu Amr and Yunus to avoid two adjacent sukuns, but the regular rule remains unless broader Arabic usage establishes an exception.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماينصبفىالألف)#57/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | After the interrogative hamza, a fronted object is accusative through an understood verb reconstructed from the clause; accusative is the preferred, standard construction.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماينصبفىالألف)#57/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A clause beginning with a noun related to the fronted noun can be parsed like a new nominal clause; making that related noun an object licenses accusative on the initial noun.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماينصبفىالألف)#57/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Raising is also possible in forms such as a fronted noun with a prepositional verb, and is stronger with marartu bihi than with a direct object construction because the initial noun can be a topic.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماينصبفىالألف)#57/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | If the fronted noun is analyzed as governed by the hidden verb, a verb requiring a preposition should make it genitive; overt and understood words otherwise share their governance.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماينصبفىالألف)#57/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In conditional senses, ḥaythu and idhā make a following noun accusative when a verb follows, but allow a nominative noun when followed by a nominal predicate.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماينصبفىالألف)#57/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Idh permits an initial nominative noun, especially with a present-tense predicate; a past-tense predicate is awkward because idh is used in obligatory narrative contexts.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماينصبفىالألف)#57/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A fronted noun is accusative when the later coordinated phrase is semantically connected to it, as through a shared description; without that connection, the construction is not valid.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماينصبفىالألف)#57/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The omitted verb has the same interpretation as the overt explanatory verb used in comparable noninterrogative fronting.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماينصبفىالألف)#57/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When the clause subject is related to the fronted noun, that subject's nominative case makes the fronted noun nominative; an unrelated object instead takes accusative.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماينصبفىالألف)#57/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | If the related noun is made the object and another noun the subject, the initial noun becomes accusative, as in the switch from Zayd as subject to his brother as object.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماينصبفىالألف)#57/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A fronted noun with a following prepositional phrase is case-marked as though the verb governed it directly; removing the phrase reveals the accusative pattern.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماينصبفىالألف)#57/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A fronted noun followed by a passive or intransitive verb plus a preposition must be nominative when the clause without that phrase is nominative.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماينصبفىالألف)#57/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | An omitted word retains the case governance it would have if expressed, whether genitive, accusative, or nominative.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماينصبفىالألف)#57/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When the interrogative hamza falls on a pronoun starting a new clause, nominative is ordinary, though accusative fronting remains good Arabic.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماينصبفىالألف)#57/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A time adverb does not separate the interrogative from the object: the object remains accusative when fronted before a verb followed by an adverbial phrase.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنأهلالحجازيقولونإذاقالالرجلرأيتزيدامنزيداوإذاقال#454/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · أهل الحجاز | reports | The Hijazis answer من زيدا? with the questioned accusative form, repeating the case used in the question as quotation.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنأهلالحجازيقولونإذاقالالرجلرأيتزيدامنزيداوإذاقال#454/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · بنو تميم | prefers | Tamim speakers answer in the nominative in every case; Sībawayh says this is more analogical than the Hijazi quotation.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنأهلالحجازيقولونإذاقالالرجلرأيتزيدامنزيداوإذاقال#454/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The Hijazi quotation is allowed for a dominant proper name because it is the most-used identifying name; it is not extended to ordinary names, and a kunya behaves like a name.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنأهلالحجازيقولونإذاقالالرجلرأيتزيدامنزيداوإذاقال#454/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | For رأيت أخا خالد, the expected answer is nominative because the name is not dominant; accusative is possible only by the quoted-name pattern.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنأهلالحجازيقولونإذاقالالرجلرأيتزيدامنزيداوإذاقال#454/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · يونس | reports | Yunus returns coordinated names to the nominative by analogy and treats زيد بن عمرو as one name, quoting the compound without tanwin; a separate adjective such as الطويل is raised.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنأهلالحجازيقولونإذاقالالرجلرأيتزيدامنزيداوإذاقال#454/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some speakers extend quotation across coordinated words; Sībawayh accepts the form, but when من separates the second phrase, أخو زيد is raised as an independent answer.
[SIBAWAYH:اعلمأنأهلالحجازيقولونإذاقالالرجلرأيتزيدامنزيداوإذاقال#454/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | If a conjunction is added before من, the response after it must be nominative; only من itself regularly permits quotation.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلك[قولك]واثلاثةوثلاثيناه|وإنلمتندبقلتياثلاثةوثلاثين#317/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The numeral phrase ثلاثة وثلاثين is one vocative unit, not two independently addressed nouns; like ثلاثة عشر, it therefore takes accusative form.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلك[قولك]واثلاثةوثلاثيناه|وإنلمتندبقلتياثلاثةوثلاثين#317/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A phrase such as يا ضاربا رجلا is definite in address, but tanwin remains because the noun phrase is not complete until رجلا.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلك[قولك]واثلاثةوثلاثيناه|وإنلمتندبقلتياثلاثةوثلاثين#317/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Tanwin also remains in يا خيرا منك because the final word is not the end of the addressed name; deletion applies only at the name's end.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلك[قولك]واثلاثةوثلاثيناه|وإنلمتندبقلتياثلاثةوثلاثين#317/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Dropping tanwin for lightness does not change the intended tanwin meaning, just as deletion does not alter the agent in ضاربك قاعدا.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلك[قولك]واثلاثةوثلاثيناه|وإنلمتندبقلتياثلاثةوثلاثين#317/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In يا أخا رجل, أخا is indefinite because it is annexed to an indefinite; رجل is not a vocative here and cannot be treated as a silently definite noun.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكأزيداأنتضاربهوأزيداأنتضاربلهوأعمراأنتمكرمأخاه#59/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Active participles such as ḍārib and munzil operate like finite verbs, allowing arguments to precede them and allowing arguments to be expressed or understood.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكأزيداأنتضاربهوأزيداأنتضاربلهوأعمراأنتمكرمأخاه#59/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | These verbal intensives differ from nominal descriptions such as ḥasan wajh al-akh: the latter cannot be inverted, pronominalized, or split like an operative participle.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكأزيداأنتضاربهوأزيداأنتضاربلهوأعمراأنتمكرمأخاه#59/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Verbal nouns can govern like verbs; Sībawayh cites the lines with يمررون, ندل, and ضرب to show verbal nouns taking verbal arguments.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكأزيداأنتضاربهوأزيداأنتضاربلهوأعمراأنتمكرمأخاه#59/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Names such as rasūl, ʿadīl, jalīs, and amīr are not action-intensifying participles, so a preceding interrogative noun remains nominative.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكأزيداأنتضاربهوأزيداأنتضاربلهوأعمراأنتمكرمأخاه#59/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A time expression with a nonverbal title such as amīr is nominative, u

nlike the same adverb before an operative verb; it is not governed by an action.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكأزيداأنتضاربهوأزيداأنتضاربلهوأعمراأنتمكرمأخاه#59/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Plural active participles on fawāʿil behave like feminine singular participles; Sībawayh cites Abū Kabīr's ʿawāqid and al-Aʿajjāj's awālif.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكأزيداأنتضاربهوأزيداأنتضاربلهوأعمراأنتمكرمأخاه#59/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · بعضهم | reports | Some speakers treat faʿʿāl as equivalent to fawʿal in plural usage, as in qaṭṭān of Mecca and sukkān of the Sacred Territory.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكأزيداأنتضاربهوأزيداأنتضاربلهوأعمراأنتمكرمأخاه#59/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Intensive agent forms operate like fāʿil when they convey an intensified action; common patterns include faʿūl, faʿʿāl, mifʿāl, and fiʿl.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكأزيداأنتضاربهوأزيداأنتضاربلهوأعمراأنتمكرمأخاه#59/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Faʿīl forms such as raḥīm, ʿalīm, qadīr, samīʿ, and baṣīr can share fāʿil's argument order and omission patterns.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكأزيداأنتضاربهوأزيداأنتضاربلهوأعمراأنتمكرمأخاه#59/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Poems by Dhū al-Rumma, Abū Dhuʾayb, and al-Qilākh show intensive participles such as هجّوم, هيوج, and لبّاس taking the flexible syntax of fāʿil.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكأزيداأنتضاربهوأزيداأنتضاربلهوأعمراأنتمكرمأخاه#59/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The spoken phrase أما العسل فأنا شراب and poems with ḍarūb, including a line by Abū Ṭālib, further attest intensive forms used like active participles.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكأزيداأنتضاربهوأزيداأنتضاربلهوأعمراأنتمكرمأخاه#59/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The fiʿl pattern is much rarer than faʿīl; ʿAmr ibn Aḥmar's misḥal is one poetic example.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكأزيداأنتضاربهوأزيداأنتضاربلهوأعمراأنتمكرمأخاه#59/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Sībawayh adduces forms from Ṭarafa, an unnamed poet, Ruʾbah, Sāʿidah ibn Juʾayyah, and al-Kumayt as further examples of intensive fiʿl forms.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكعجبتمنضربزيدافمعناهأنهيضربزيدا|وتقولعجبتمنضرب#79/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A verbal noun such as ḍarb Zaydan means an understood finite clause; unlike an active participle, it does not state its agent, so agent and object may both need expression.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكعجبتمنضربزيدافمعناهأنهيضربزيدا|وتقولعجبتمنضرب#79/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A verbal noun can take a time adverb, as in عجبت من ضرب اليوم زيدا; poetry contrasts this with اليوم in a nonverbal nominal phrase.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكعجبتمنضربزيدافمعناهأنهيضربزيدا|وتقولعجبتمنضرب#79/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The Qurʾanic infinitive iṭʿām governs the object yatīman, illustrating the verbal noun's ability to take an object. | mentions 90:14, 90:15
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكعجبتمنضربزيدافمعناهأنهيضربزيدا|وتقولعجبتمنضرب#79/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With tanwīn, a verbal noun can take overt agent and patient nouns in either role, corresponding to an understood finite clause.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكعجبتمنضربزيدافمعناهأنهيضربزيدا|وتقولعجبتمنضرب#79/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | If tanwīn is omitted, the following noun is genitive and substitutes for it; that noun may represent either the verbal noun's agent or its object.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكعجبتمنضربزيدافمعناهأنهيضربزيدا|وتقولعجبتمنضرب#79/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A verbal noun can coordinate agent and patient nouns as an active participle does; Ruʾbah's lines illustrate this governing construction.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكعجبتمنضربزيدافمعناهأنهيضربزيدا|وتقولعجبتمنضرب#79/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With the definite article, the verbal noun can govern an accusative object like an active participle; Sībawayh cites poetry including a line by al-Murār al-Asadī.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكعجبتمنضربزيدافمعناهأنهيضربزيدا|وتقولعجبتمنضرب#79/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | rejects | Sībawayh rejects الضرب الرجل as nonstandard because it resembles an adjectival phrase; al-Khalīl accepts a broader construction by analogy with ḥasan al-akh.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكعجبتمنضربزيدافمعناهأنهيضربزيدا|وتقولعجبتمنضرب#79/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl accepts by analogy a verbal-noun construction modeled on the adjectival phrase, though Sībawayh says this is not ordinary speech.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكعجبتمنضربزيدافمعناهأنهيضربزيدا|وتقولعجبتمنضرب#79/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | An unarticled verbal noun may be annexed with or without tanwīn, whether the action actually occurred or not.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكلارجلاليومظريفاولارجلفيهاعاقلاإذاجعلتفيها#357/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In لا رجل اليوم ظريفا and لا رجل فيها عاقلا, the adjective is tanwinned when a word intervenes; noun and adjective cannot be treated as one word across that separation.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكلارجلاليومظريفاولارجلفيهاعاقلاإذاجعلتفيها#357/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | An annexed noun such as ماء سماء is not compounded with what follows like خمسة عشر, so its adjective follows the usual pattern and remains tanwinned.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكلارجلاليومظريفاولارجلفيهاعاقلاإذاجعلتفيها#357/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When tanwin is removed because of annexation, the adjective follows the ordinary annexed construction, as in لا ضاربا زيدا لك and لا حسنا وجه الأخ فيها.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكلارجلاليومظريفاولارجلفيهاعاقلاإذاجعلتفيها#357/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | After لا ماء ولا لبن, the adjective for لبن may be tanwinned or not; if it describes ماء it must be tanwinned because the paired words form one unit needing a predicate.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكلارجلاليومظريفاولارجلفيهاعاقلاإذاجعلتفيها#357/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In لا أبا لك, an omitted locative element is understood.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكلهعلىألفدرهمعرفاms158|ومثلذلكقولالأحوص#177/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | These accusative verbal nouns emphasize an already stated action or assertion; the construction is neither an adjective nor an object governed by a preceding noun, and it uses an understood verb.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكلهعلىألفدرهمعرفاms158|ومثلذلكقولالأحوص#177/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In the shepherd's poem, وجيف المطايا emphasizes the earlier implied verb أوجفت, continuing the same pattern of an omitted verb replaced by its verbal noun.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكلهعلىألفدرهمعرفاms158|ومثلذلكقولالأحوص#177/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Tanwin or an indefinite verbal noun can reinforce an earlier assertion: عرفا follows an acknowledgment, while the poet's قسما reinforces an oath, like سيرا after سير عليه.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكلهعلىألفدرهمعرفاms158|ومثلذلكقولالأحوص#177/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Emphatic verbal nouns may take the definite article or annexation, as in صنع الله, وعد الله, and خلقه; these forms work like the other verbal nouns in this construction. | mentions 27:88, 30:5, 30:6, 32:7
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكلهعلىألفدرهمعرفاms158|ومثلذلكقولالأحوص#177/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A nominative reading is also possible by supplying an implied noun, as in ذاك وعد الله, or an implied copula, as in هو دعوة الحق.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكلأنهمبدءوابالإضمارلأنهمشرطواالتفسيروذلكنووافجرىذلكفي#285/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In praise constructions, the accusative after نعم is analyzed like the accusative after حسبك به or ويحه, with comparable praise force.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكلأنهمبدءوابالإضمارلأنهمشرطواالتفسيروذلكنووافجرىذلكفي#285/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The plural subject marker is not shown after نعم; speakers rely on its following explanation, and frequent use fixes this deletion as with بئس. | mentions 27:87
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكلأنهمبدءوابالإضمارلأنهمشرطواالتفسيروذلكنووافجرىذلكفي#285/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | نعم and بئس derive from نعم and بئس and function as verbs only for praise and blame, respectively.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكلأنهمبدءوابالإضمارلأنهمشرطواالتفسيروذلكنووافجرىذلكفي#285/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In هذه الدار نعمت البلد, the feminine marker follows البلد understood as الدار; when البلد is masculine, نعم البلد is also used.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكلأنهمبدءوابالإضمارلأنهمشرطواالتفسيروذلكنووافجرىذلكفي#285/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A poet uses masculine فيه with الدار because the house is construed as a place, showing agreement can follow that sense.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكلأنهمبدءوابالإضمارلأنهمشرطواالتفسيروذلكنووافجرىذلكفي#285/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil analyzes حبذا as a single unit like حب الشيء; ذا remains masculine because the compound has become a fixed idiom.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكلأنهمبدءوابالإضمارلأنهمشرطواالتفسيروذلكنووافجرىذلكفي#285/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | أيما can modify an indefinite, serve as a circumstantial qualifier with a definite, or function interrogatively; it does not mark number or introduce an exception.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكلأنهمبدءوابالإضمارلأنهمشرطواالتفسيروذلكنووافجرىذلكفي#285/r16] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | أيما فتى is interrogative, with an element of astonishment, as shown by the comparable questions سبحان الله من هو وما هو.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكلأنهمبدءوابالإضمارلأنهمشرطواالتفسيروذلكنووافجرىذلكفي#285/r17] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | أحد and the listed words occur under negation, not as affirmative predicates, circumstantials, exceptions, or classifiers that specify a type or number.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكلأنهمبدءوابالإضمارلأنهمشرطواالتفسيروذلكنووافجرىذلكفي#285/r18] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | After عسل ملء جرة or دين شعر كلبين, رفع is the normal analysis because the following noun is an adjective; نصب is also possible after a complete clause.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكلأنهمبدءوابالإضمارلأنهمشرطواالتفسيروذلكنووافجرىذلكفي#285/r19] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In عليها مثلها زبد, زبد may be a بدل or an answer equivalent to هو زبد, but it is not an adjective because it is a noun.

[SIBAWAYH:وذلكلأنهمبدءوابالإضمارلأنهمشرطواالتفسيروذلكنووافجرىذلكفي#285/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In نعم الرجل عبد الله, نعم governs الرجل rather than عبد الله; reversing the order gives a separate clause identifying what عبد الله is like.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكلأنهمبدءوابالإضمارلأنهمشرطواالتفسيروذلكنووافجرىذلكفي#285/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | نعم can govern a hidden element explained afterward, or can govern an overt noun directly; the two patterns parallel ويحه and ربه.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكلأنهمبدءوابالإضمارلأنهمشرطواالتفسيروذلكنووافجرىذلكفي#285/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The person identified after نعم الرجل must be the same person denoted by الرجل; عبد الله نعم الرجل cannot mean the man is someone else.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكلأنهمبدءوابالإضمارلأنهمشرطواالتفسيروذلكنووافجرىذلكفي#285/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | الرجل after نعم names a praiseworthy class: the speaker places the individual among a whole group of good people rather than identifying a particular man by his quality.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكلأنهمبدءوابالإضمارلأنهمشرطواالتفسيروذلكنووافجرىذلكفي#285/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A plural group cannot be praised by splitting its members as نعم صغارهم وكبارهم; acceptable forms name the classes or praise the group as a whole.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكلأنهمبدءوابالإضمارلأنهمشرطواالتفسيروذلكنووافجرىذلكفي#285/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When نعم governs an overt noun, that noun is definite or annexed, as in الرجل or غلام الرجل, while referring to a class rather than a specific individual.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكلأنهمبدءوابالإضمارلأنهمشرطواالتفسيروذلكنووافجرىذلكفي#285/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | نعم may be masculine or feminine: نعمت المرأة is more frequent, though نعم المرأة is also said.
[FARRA:v1p259/r5] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | أن تجمعوا بين الأختين is nominative in sense, like the verbal noun الجمع بين الأختين.
[MAJAZ:v1p121/r10] MAJAZ, d. 209 · author | holds | The same accusative construction appears in ṣabran, mahlan, and ḥallan, meaning “be patient,” “wait,” and “loosen.”

[TAB-FULL:v6p556/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The women named in the passage are forbidden to marry by unanimous agreement, though early Companions disagreed about a wife’s mother if the daughter was divorced before consummation.
[TAB-FULL:v6p556/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | All early and later scholars hold a wife’s mother forbidden whether or not the husband consummated the marriage; the entry condition applies only to stepdaughters, not mothers-in-law.

[TAB-FULL:v6p556/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · بعض المتقدمين | reports | Some early authorities held it lawful to marry a wife’s mother if the marriage to her daughter ended before consummation, treating her like a stepdaughter.

[BAQILLANI:v1p153/r1] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · قس بن ساعدة | reports | The sermon attributed to Quss ibn Sāʿida reflects on mortality, vanished peoples, changing fortune, and the return of what has passed.

[BAQILLANI:v1p153/r3] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Comparing early sermons, reports, and eloquent speech with the Qurʾān lets readers recognize how Qurʾānic composition differs from all human discourse.
[BAQILLANI:v1p153/r4] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · القائل | reports | A possible objection says poetry surpasses sermons, letters, and ordinary conversation in eloquence and therefore seems the closest human comparison to the Qurʾān.
[BAQILLANI:v1p206/r1] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | The Qurʾān’s style remains consistent across varied structures, connections, openings, endings, and rhetorical paths.

[BAQILLANI:v1p206/r3] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Human speech changes tone and quality, mixing splendid and ugly wording, incongruous lines, and disordered composition; two poetic sayings illustrate such defects.
[BAQILLANI:v1p206/r4] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | reports | A hypothetical objection says some Qurʾānic passages do not display brilliance in individual words, but only in the overall passage.
[BAQILLANI:v1p206/r5] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | The list of forbidden relatives is necessarily a sequence of names, so its eloquence lies instead in its arrangement and the wisdom of its meaning.
[BAQILLANI:v1p207/r1] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | The verse begins with mothers because they have the greatest inviolability, are directly related through birth, and are the nearest of the listed kin.

[BAQILLANI:v1p207/r3] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Mentioning milk sisters after milk mothers signals other relations derived through nursing and places sisters next to mothers in the sequence.
[BAQILLANI:v1p207/r4] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | The author leaves the verse’s full legal discussion to a projected book on Qurʾānic meanings, since that is outside this work’s scope.
[BAQILLANI:v1p207/r5] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | The verse’s legal wisdom compensates where inimitability cannot appear in individual words; its order and linked wording still display Qurʾānic eloquence.
[BAQILLANI:v1p207/r6] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Names can make poetry effective or damage its meter and flow; Abu Dhuʾayb’s named-kin line is offered as an instance of successful placement.
[BAQILLANI:v1p207/r7] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Legal verses must use the terms their rulings require, yet whenever rhetorical freedom remains, the Qurʾān reaches unsurpassed eloquence through words, phrases, transitions, and endings.
[BAQILLANI:v1p207/r8] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | holds | Careful readers recognize the Qurʾān’s distinctive mode and genre through the direction and endpoint of its discourse.

[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p32/r14] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | rejects | Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects extending the condition to wives’ mothers on grammatical grounds: genitives with different governors cannot share an adjective.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p32/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Nieces of brothers and sisters include full, paternal, and maternal sibling relations.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p32/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · أبو حيوة | reports | Abū Ḥaywa reads al-riḍāʿa with kasra on rāʾ; breastfeeding creates the same marriage prohibitions as lineage.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p32/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The nursing mother is a mother; her children, born before or after, are siblings, as are the milk-father’s children.

 · ابن عباس | reports | A similar view is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, though another report from him agrees with the majority.

[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v2p33/r8] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | If he has intercourse with one and then unexpectedly with the other, both are suspended until he prohibits one, because he is now suspect.

[TABRISI:4:23#2/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | A mother includes every woman connected to a person through childbirth, whether the line runs through the father or mother and through women or men.

[TABRISI:4:23#2/r4] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Paternal aunts include sisters of any male ancestor on the father's side and also sisters of the mother's father and maternal grandfathers above him.

[TABRISI:4:23#2/r6] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The plural address and possessive make each prohibited relative correspond to each individual addressed, prohibiting every person's own mother, daughter, and the like.
[TABRISI:4:23#2/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The plural prohibitions on brothers' and sisters' daughters likewise correspond person by person, and their limits match those for biological daughters.
[TABRISI:4:23#2/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās says seven women are prohibited by affinity and identifies the seventh as women married by one's fathers, citing 4:22. | mentions 4:22
[TABRISI:4:23#2/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | A milk mother includes the woman who nursed a person, a woman who nursed that person's wet nurse, or a woman who nursed a man using her husband's or master's milk; women who bore the nurse are also milk mothers.

[TABRISI:4:23#3/r11] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The prohibition on a wife's mother includes her grandmothers, near or distant, by lineage or nursing, and takes effect upon contracting marriage with the daughter, even without consummation.
[TABRISI:4:23#3/r12] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Rabāʾib are the wives' daughters from other men; ḥujūr means the husband's guardianship and upbringing.

[TABRISI:4:23#3/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · بعض أصحابنا | reports | Some of the author's school instead require ten consecutive nursing sessions.
[TABRISI:4:23#4/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Being in the husband's household is not a legal condition for prohibiting a stepdaughter; scholars agree, and the wording reflects the usual situation.
[TABRISI:4:23#4/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The wives of biological sons are prohibited; the phrase “from your loins” clarifies that a wife of an adopted son is not thereby prohibited.

[TABRISI:4:23#4/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The prohibition covers a wife's daughter by another husband and her descendants, whether near or distant.

[RAZI-FULL:v10p21/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The verse names fourteen forbidden categories: seven through blood relationship, and seven otherwise—foster mothers and sisters, wives' mothers, consummated wives' daughters, sons' wives, fathers' wives (in the prior verse), and combining two sisters. | mentions 4:22
[RAZI-FULL:v10p21/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الكرخي | reports | Al-Karkhī calls the verse ambiguous because prohibition is attached to persons rather than an explicitly named act, and no act is stated as its object.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p21/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Al-Razi rejects the ambiguity claim: the preceding prohibition of marrying fathers' former wives (4:22) makes marriage the intended prohibited act here. | mentions 4:22
[RAZI-FULL:v10p21/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Ordinary usage and necessary religious knowledge identify the prohibited act when permission or prohibition is attached to persons: eating carrion and blood, marrying mothers and daughters, and shedding a Muslim's blood.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p22#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Mothers and daughters have been forbidden from Adam's time onward in every revealed religion; Zoroaster, whom most Muslims considered a liar, reportedly allowed them.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p22#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Sister marriage was reportedly permitted in Adam's time as a necessity.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p22#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعض المشايخ | rejects | Some shaykhs deny that Adam's children married their sisters and say God sent houris from Paradise to marry his sons.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p22#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Al-Razi calls that account implausible: if their wives and their daughters' husbands came from Paradise, Adam's descendants would not be exclusively his children, contrary to consensus.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p22#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Intercourse is degrading: people are ashamed to mention it, do it in seclusion, and use it in many insults; mothers deserve protection because their benefaction to children is greatest.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p22#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A daughter is part of a person, as the Prophet says of Fāṭima, so intercourse with her is likewise degrading and she must be protected.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p22#2/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Al-Wāḥidī explains that ummāt is a plural of umm, whose original form was ummah; the hāʾ was dropped in the singular.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p22#2/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · شاعر | reports | A cited line uses the plural ummahāt and names Khindif as the poet's mother and Iyās as his father.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p22/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Because the clause is passive, it does not expressly name God as the agent of prohibition; that must be supplied by consensus, so the verse alone proves nothing further.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p22/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The wording does not specify that the prohibition lasts forever; permanence requires evidence beyond the verse's apparent wording.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p22/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | As direct address, the wording appears limited to those present, so applying the rule to everyone requires separate evidence.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p22/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | As a past-tense report, the wording does not itself cover the present or future; that extension needs separate evidence.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p22/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The plural wording superficially says each person is forbidden every mother and daughter, whereas the intended distributive sense pairs each person with his own mother and daughter.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p22/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The past form suggests a new prohibition after prior permissibility; if these relations had always been forbidden, it would imply re-creating an existing prohibition, so separate evidence is needed.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p23/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الراعي | reports | Al-Rāʿī's verse uses ummāt for animal mothers, illustrating that this plural is especially common for nonhuman animals.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p23/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A mother includes every woman in one's birth ancestry, through one or more generations and through either female or male links.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p23/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | If umm is a univocal term shared literally by one's immediate mother and all grandmothers, the verse explicitly prohibits marrying both.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p23/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | If umm is homonymous for mother and grandmother, those who allow one shared expression to carry both senses make the verse explicit about prohibiting all grandmothers too.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p23/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Those who forbid using a homonym for both senses either take the verse to mean only the immediate mother, leaving grandmother prohibition to consensus, or posit two divine utterances with distinct senses.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p23/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The same interpretive options apply if the word is literal for the immediate mother but metaphorical for grandmothers, since one word cannot simultaneously carry its literal and figurative senses.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p23/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shāfiʿī requires the legal penalty for a man who marries and consummates marriage with his mother; Abū Ḥanīfa does not.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p23/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shāfiʿī argues that such a marriage is void and the intercourse is therefore unqualified zinā, requiring the penalty in 24:2; its offer and acceptance cannot form a valid contract, and scripture categorically invalidates it. | mentions 24:2
[RAZI-FULL:v10p24#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The forbidden sisters include full sisters, paternal half-sisters, and maternal half-sisters.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p24#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الواحدي | reports | Al-Wāḥidī defines a paternal aunt as the sister of any male ancestor, including a mother's father's sister; a maternal aunt is a sister of any female ancestor, including a father's mother's sister.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p24#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Nieces through brothers and sisters follow the same rule as daughters descended directly from oneself.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p24#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · المفسرون | reports | The seven blood-relationship categories are expressly prohibited and, according to the commentators, can never become lawful.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p24#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The rest of the verse names women who would otherwise be lawful but become prohibited through a temporary circumstance.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p24/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A daughter is every female descended from a person by birth through one or more generations, through either female or male links.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p24/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Whether a son's or daughter's daughter is literally or figuratively called a daughter is the same lexical question discussed for grandmothers.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p24/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shāfiʿī holds that a daughter conceived through fornication is not forbidden to the fornicator; Abū Ḥanīfa holds that she is.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p24/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shāfiʿī argues that biological conception cannot establish paternity consistently under Abū Ḥanīfa's rules: a child of a purchased virgin may lack paternity, while a child of distant spouses has it despite no biological conception by the husband.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p24/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shāfiʿī argues that legal lineage from adultery is denied by Muslim consensus, and a judge would have to prevent the child from claiming the fornicator as her father.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p24/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | Al-Shāfiʿī cites the Prophet's rule that a child belongs to the marital bed and the adulterer receives the stone, restricting lineage to the marriage bed.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p24/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shāfiʿī infers she is not his daughter because she inherits (4:11), could be subject to his marriage guardianship, and would be owed maintenance and custody; none applies, and solitude with her would be permitted. | mentions 4:11
[RAZI-FULL:v10p24/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Since she is not his daughter and fornication does not create affinity prohibition either, she is not forbidden to marry him.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p25#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shāfiʿī requires five nursing sessions for prohibition; Abū Ḥanīfa considers even one session sufficient.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p25#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو بكر الرازي | reports | Abū Bakr al-Rāzī argues that the verse ties maternal or sibling status to nursing, so any occurrence of nursing should trigger the ruling.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p25#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو بكر الرازي | reports | He answers an objection that ‘mothers who clothed you’ would imply prior motherhood: nursing itself confers the maternal name, unlike clothing.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p25#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ابن عمر | reports | When told that Ibn al-Zubayr allowed one or two feeds, Ibn ʿUmar answered that God's ruling is better and cited foster sisters, understanding the verse to prohibit even little nursing.

[RAZI-FULL:v10p25/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Although the verse expressly names foster mothers and sisters, the Prophet's rule extends the prohibition of nursing to every relation forbidden by blood kinship.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p25/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Naming a nursing mother and sister signals that nursing follows lineage: of seven blood-prohibited classes, two arise through birth and five through sibling relationships; the verse names one example from each group, and the hadith confirms the inference.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p25/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A milk-mother is the woman who nursed someone and any woman maternally related to her through birth or nursing; the same applies to the milk-father and the descendants treated as daughters.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p25/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A full foster sister shares both milk parents: she is a stranger nursed by one's mother with one's father's milk, whether nursed at the same time or before or after.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p25/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A paternal foster sister shares one's father but not one's mother: one's father's wife nursed her with his milk.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p25/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A maternal foster sister shares one's mother but not one's father: one's mother nursed her with another man's milk.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p25/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Once foster parents are defined, the same method identifies foster aunts, uncles, nieces, and nephews.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p26/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The prohibition of a wife's mother includes her original mother and all grandmothers through either parent, as with lineage generally.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p26/r10] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A possible reply is that 'min' means connection in both clauses, as in the verse describing believing men and women as allies of one another. | mentions 9:71
[RAZI-FULL:v10p26/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الأكثرين من الصحابة والتابعين | reports | The majority of Companions and Successors hold that marrying a woman prohibits her mother whether or not the marriage is consummated.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p26/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · علي وزيد وابن عمر وابن الزبير وجابر وابن عباس | reports | A group of Companions, including Ali, Zayd, Ibn Umar, Ibn al-Zubayr, Jabir, and according to the strongest reports Ibn Abbas, hold that the mother is forbidden only after intercourse with the daughter, like a stepdaughter.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p26/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · جمع من الصحابة | reports | Their grammatical argument is that the verse states two rulings and then one condition, so the condition applies to both rulings.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p26/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | The author favors the majority: 'your wives' mothers' is an independent clause, and no proof makes the later condition govern it.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p26/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A condition must attach to something already stated; attaching it to one clause suffices, while extending it to the other abandons the apparent wording without proof.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p26/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The clause's general meaning is certain, whereas the condition's return to it is only a possibility; restricting the generality on that uncertain basis is impermissible.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p26/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | If the condition applies only to mothers-in-law, stepdaughters would be forbidden without consummation, which consensus rejects.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p26/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | If it applies to both clauses, 'min' would have to mean 'from among' for mothers-in-law and origin for stepdaughters, improperly giving one word two senses.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p27#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A stepdaughter (rabiba) is a man's wife's daughter by another man; the word means one brought up because the man raises her, and the two cited verbs have the same meaning.

[RAZI-FULL:v10p27#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · سائر العلماء | reports | Other scholars hold that consummation with the mother forbids her daughter whether or not she was raised by the husband, because the verse makes absence of consummation the basis for there being no blame.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p27#2/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | The author rejects care as a legal condition: the verse mentions the usual case, since a wife's daughter is ordinarily raised by her husband.

[RAZI-FULL:v10p27/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · عبدالله بن مسعود | reports | Ibn Masud once permitted marrying a woman's mother after divorcing her before intercourse; after seeing the people of Medina united against his ruling, he returned to Kufa and ordered a man to leave that wife.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p27/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · زيد بن ثابت | reports | Zayd ibn Thabit says that after divorce before consummation a man may marry his wife's mother, but after her death he may not.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p27/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The author explains that divorce before consummation carries no rulings of consummation, including no waiting period, while death counts like consummation for the waiting-period rule and therefore triggers this prohibition.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p28#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shafii prohibits a father from marrying his son's slave woman, whereas Abu Hanifa permits it.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p28#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shafii's argument is that the son's slave woman is his halila, and the verse prohibits a son's halila to his father.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p28#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The author derives halila from permissibility, making it a woman made lawful, and from hulul, making it a place where the master resides; both cover a slave woman.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p28#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The author gives two further derivations: the pair is as if settled together in one garment, cover, or home, or each settled in the other's heart and spirit through love and intimacy.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p28#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The conventional phrase 'a man's halila' meaning his wife does not exclude a slave woman; defining the word broadly to include both defeats the contrary linguistic claim, which is only negative testimony.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p28#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | 'From your loins' excludes an adopted son: early Islam treated an adopted child as a son, but the wife of a man merely claimed as a son is not forbidden if he is not his biological son.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p28#2/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | After Zayd ibn Haritha divorced Zaynab bint Jahsh, the Prophet married her; the polytheists accused him of marrying his son's wife, and the cited verses denied that adoption makes adopted sons true sons and removed blame from marrying their former wives. | mentions 33:4, 33:37
[RAZI-FULL:v10p28/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو بكر الرازي | reports | Abu Bakr al-Razi argues that adultery creates affinity prohibitions: 'entering' a woman means intercourse whether lawful or illicit, so adultery with a mother forbids her daughter.

s is likewise excluded from a bequest to a man's wives and from a legally binding oath about a family's wives, reinforcing that she is not included in the wording.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p29/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The apparent wording excludes a milk-son's wife, while 'what is beyond these' in the next verse appears to permit her; the Prophetic rule that nursing forbids what lineage forbids specifies that general permission, so a solitary report narrows the Qur'an's general wording. | mentions 4:24
[RAZI-FULL:v10p29/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Scholars agree that a son's wife becomes forbidden to his father as soon as the marriage contract is made, whether or not the son consummated it, because the verse is general.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p29/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says to leave unspecified the condition God left unspecified; here that means the prohibition is permanent, not that the ruling is obscure, as with the seven permanently forbidden blood relations called the unspecified ones.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p29/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The prohibition also covers a grandson's wife; this shows that a grandson is called one of the grandfather's loins and is descended from him.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p30#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | The cited permissions do not permit combining the sisters even in intercourse: Muslims agree intercourse with both is forbidden, and if ownership of both permitted intercourse by the cited rule, it would be permitted, which it is not. | mentions 70:29, 70:30, 23:5, 23:6
[RAZI-FULL:v10p30#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The author reports the Prophetic rule that when the forbidden and permitted meet, the forbidden prevails, supporting the prohibition of combining them in ownership.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p30#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The author also invokes the Prophetic advice to leave what causes doubt for what does not.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p30#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | prefers | Ali's position is favored by caution: sexual relations are presumptively forbidden, and when evidence about a contract's conditions is balanced, prohibition is required; the lawfulness of marriage is an exception to that baseline.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p30#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The author reasons that if sexual relations lacked humiliation and harm, marriage to mothers would be lawful because serving them benefits them; its prohibition shows the practice entails harm, so prohibition is the baseline and lawfulness an exception. | mentions 2:83
[RAZI-FULL:v10p30#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Under the better-known juristic view, a man may own two enslaved sisters, but intercourse with one makes the other forbidden until he relinquishes ownership of the first by sale, gift, emancipation, manumission contract, or marriage.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p30/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The phrase 'and combining two sisters' is grammatically nominative, with an implied sense: forbidden to you are your mothers, daughters, and combining two sisters.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p30/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Combining two sisters occurs through marrying both, owning both, or marrying one while owning the other; simultaneous marriage to both raises the possible rulings of upholding the union, choosing one, allowing later choice, or voiding it.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p30/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The simultaneous marriage is void under the verse; this challenges Abu Hanifa's principle that prohibition does not entail invalidity, illustrated by prohibited triple divorce, exchanging one dirham for two, and other corrupt sales.
[RAZI-FULL:v10p30/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Although someone might compare this to prohibited divorce during menstruation or a post-menstrual purity in which intercourse occurred, the author says a subtle distinction between the cases is explained in his work on disputed issues.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p579/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Milk kinship maps through the wet nurse and her husband: his parents are grandparents, his sister an aunt, his other children paternal siblings, and her children by him full siblings.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p579/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Two exceptions to the nursing rule are marrying one's nursing son's sister or nursing brother's mother, since the intercourse that creates the corresponding lineage bar is absent.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p579/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The verse does not settle nursing age, number of feeds, milk-father, or ways of administering milk into the stomach; jurists disagree on these matters.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p579/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Most read اللاتي أرضعنكم; ʿAbd Allāh reads اللاي, Ibn Hurmuz التي, and Abū Ḥaywah reads الرضاعة with a kasra on rāʾ.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p579/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الجمهور | reports | Most authorities take mothers of wives as an unrestricted prohibition, whether or not the marriage to the daughter was consummated.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p579/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · علي ومجاهد | reports | ʿAlī, Mujāhid, and others allow marrying a wife's mother if the wife was divorced before consummation, treating her like a stepdaughter.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p579/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · علي وداود وأهل الظاهر | reports | They read “stepdaughters in your care” as a condition: if the daughter was not in his care, a man who consummated with her mother may marry her; both custody and consummation must be present for prohibition.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p580/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الطحاوي وغيره | reports | They explain the stepdaughters' association with the household as describing the usual case; stepdaughters remain forbidden even when they are not actually in the man's custody.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p580/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari takes “in your households” as explaining the prohibition: the girls are or may be raised by you, and after intercourse with their mothers they function like your own daughters.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p580/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The phrase “from your wives who you have entered” appears to modify only the stepdaughters clause.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p580/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The relative pronoun modifies the wives governed by من, not the wives in “mothers of your wives,” because the two phrases have different grammatical governors.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p580/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The phrase cannot be attached to an omitted element governing both mothers-in-law and stepdaughters: من identifies which wives for the former but marks origin for the latter.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p580/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari proposes attaching من نسائكم to both wives and stepdaughters, taking من to mean connection, as in the verse and cited expressions. | mentions 9:71
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p580/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | Abu Hayyan says no one recognizes “connection” as a meaning of من; the cited verse, poetry, and report have other explanations, and the proposed attachment makes the mothers-in-law phrase redundant and unidiomatic.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p581/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Entering upon a woman is a euphemism for intercourse, as in expressions meaning that a man built over her or put a veil over her.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p581/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | “No blame if you did not enter upon them” means no blame in marrying the stepdaughters, but permission also presupposes separation from their mothers by divorce or the mothers' death.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p581/r11] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The jurists agree that a father's contracted wife is forbidden to his son and a son's contracted wife to his father, whether intercourse occurred; حليلة means wife rather than an enslaved concubine, so the contract itself suffices.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p581/r12] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | “From your loins” limits sons to biological sons and removes the metaphorical sense used for adopted sons; the verse about Muhammad not being the father of any of their men addresses that usage. | mentions 33:40
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p581/r13] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The Prophet married Zaynab bint Jahsh after Zayd ibn Harithah divorced her, and jurists agree a foster son's wife is forbidden just like a biological son's wife.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p581/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عباس وطاوس وابن دينار | reports | They take the bāʾ as causative, meaning the women brought under the covering; on this view a man divorced after the wedding but before intercourse may marry her daughter.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p581/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · عطاء ومالك وأبو حنيفة والثوري والأوزاعي والليث والشافعي | reports | These jurists, in one of al-Shafiʿi's positions, hold that touching the woman with desire makes both her mother and daughter forbidden, as well as making her forbidden to the man's father and son.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p581/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن أبي ليلى والشافعي ومالك والكوفيون | reports | On lustful looking, Ibn Abi Layla and al-Shafiʿi require touching; Malik counts looking pleasurably at hair or beauty; the Kufans count lustful looking at the genital area.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p581/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الثوري | reports | Al-Thawri says looking at her genital area is prohibitive when deliberate, without stipulating desire.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p581/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · عطاء وحماد بن أبي سليمان | reports | They say looking at a woman's genital area bars marriage to her mother or daughter, and extend this ruling to enslaved women.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p581/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الحسن | reports | Al-Hasan says an enslaved woman is never lawful for the owner's son if he has touched her lustfully, uncovered her, or kissed her.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p581/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · مسروق | reports | Masruq ordered that his enslaved woman be sold after his death, saying even his limited touching and looking had made her forbidden to his son.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p581/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · عمر | reports | Umar stripped an enslaved woman with whom he had been alone; when his son asked for her, Umar said she was not lawful to him.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p582/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | “Wives of your sons” refers to wives; merely purchasing a slave woman does not bar her to the buyer's father or son, but touching or kissing her does, while lustful looking is disputed.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p605/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Expressions imply linked rules: reluctance hints consensual inheritance transfer; the ban on coercing wives allows restraint for their benefit; the prohibition on fathers' wives recalls pre-Islamic practice; permission points to prior bans; slave-marriage conditions and human weakness point to desire.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p607/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | He calls “forbidden to you” followed by “made lawful” verbal antithesis; “chaste, not fornicators” also opposes guarding sexuality to making it freely available.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v3p607/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | “Those you have entered upon” excludes unconsummated marriages; “stepdaughters in your care” and “of women” add qualifications. The statements about faith and shared origin are parenthetical, with omissions elsewhere.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#2/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | The author rejects Abu al-Baqa's comparison: he compares broken plurals with sound plurals, although broken plurals restore the missing consonant in both أبناء and إخوة, while sound plurals omit it in both.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#2/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The ألف in خالة and خال comes from واو, as shown by th

e plural أخوال and the phrase in 24:61. | mentions 24:61
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#2/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | من الرضاعة is an accusative circumstantial phrase modifying the sisters, understood as sisters who are from nursing.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#2/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو حيوة | reports | Abu Haywa reads الرضاعة with kasra on the راء.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#2/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | من نسائكم may be a circumstantial phrase modifying ربائبكم, meaning stepdaughters from your women.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#2/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Alternatively, من نسائكم may describe the implicit pronoun in في حجوركم, because a relative clause contains a pronoun.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#2/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | ربائب is the plural of ربيبة, a spouse's daughter, and ربيب is the masculine; they are named for each spouse's rearing the other's child.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#2/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The phrase اللاتي في حجوركم does not imply a legal restriction; it reflects the usual circumstance of stepdaughters being in the household.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#2/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | حجور is the plural of حجر, with either vowel on حاء; it first means the front of a garment and then protection or shelter.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#3/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | اللاتي دخلتم بهن modifies the second نسائكم governed by من; consummation with the mother is required for the stepdaughter to be prohibited.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#3/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | It cannot modify both occurrences of نسائكم because they have different governing prepositions and a shared adjective cannot modify nouns with different governors.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#3/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | It also cannot modify both on legal grounds: mothers-in-law are prohibited by contract alone according to the majority, whereas stepdaughters require consummation with their mother.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#3/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari's explanation makes the stepdaughter prohibited only when her mother has been consummated with; without that, she remains lawful.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#3/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | If the phrase is linked to both mothers-in-law and stepdaughters, من would have to mean specification for one and source or origin for the other, an impermissible double sense in one expression.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#3/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | If linked only to mothers-in-law, the nearer stepdaughter phrase should receive it absent a compelling reason, and everyone agrees mothers-in-law are prohibited without qualification.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#3/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari allows من to mean connection and link the phrase to both women and stepdaughters, comparing the mutual relationship in 9:67 and the relationship between daughters and mothers. | mentions 9:67
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#4/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | An anonymous poem uses منك and مني to express connection between two people, offered as evidence for that sense of من.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#4/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | A second anonymous poetic line likewise uses من to express reciprocal connection.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#4/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · علي وابن عباس وزيد وابن عمرو وابن الزبير | reports | A reported reading adds اللاتي دخلتم بهن after mothers-in-law, making their prohibition conditional on consummation; Ibn Abbas reportedly swore this alone was revealed.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#4/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas reportedly swore that the conditional wording was the only revelation.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#4/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الشيخ | reports | The Shaykh says he knows no one who gives من the meaning of connection; the cited verse, poem, and report are all interpreted differently.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#5/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | حلائل is the plural of حليلة, meaning wife, named because she dwells with her husband wherever he is; it is an active feminine form.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#5/r10] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Al-Farra also cites the spoken complaint إذا أقوم اشتكى صلبي for that dialectal form.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#5/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | An anonymous poem uses حليلها for the husband, illustrating the masculine counterpart.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#5/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj and others derive حليلة from حلال, with each spouse being permitted to the other, so فعيل is passive; the author objects to the feminine ending unless it is treated as a frozen noun like نطيحة or ذبيحة.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#5/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Another derivation uses حل as the opposite of tying: each spouse undoes the other's waist wrapper.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#5/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The phrase الذين من أصلابكم clarifies that the prohibited sons' wives are those of biological sons, since son can also refer to an adopted child.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#5/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | A son through nursing has the same rule as a biological son here, established by the Sunnah and thus not a counterexample to the verse.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#5/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | أصلاب is plural of صلب, the back, named for its firmness; the Hijazi pronunciation with ḍamma then sukūn is the most eloquent.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#5/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Al-Farra reports that Tamim and Asad pronounce the word صلب with fatḥa on both consonants.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#5/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | An anonymous poem witnesses the dialectal pronunciation in the phrase في صلب.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#6/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | وأن تجمعوا is in the nominative, coordinated with the nominative element of حرمت: combining two sisters in marriage is prohibited.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#6/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Combining two sisters in ownership is unanimously allowed, while intercourse with both by right of ownership is disputed.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#6/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The exception after ما قد سلف is disconnected and accusative, meaning God forgives what occurred in pre-Islamic times.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#6/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | An alternative takes the exception as connected: a pre-Islamic marriage of two sisters remains valid after Islam, but the man must choose one and leave the other.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23#6/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | Although a similar sense was possible for the earlier ما قد سلف in 4:22, the connected exception cannot work here because it yields a false meaning. | mentions 4:22
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The common plural of أم is أمهات, with an extra ه distinguishing rational mothers from non-rational ones; an anonymous line illustrates أمات for young animals.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23/r10] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · أبو البقاء | reports | Abu al-Baqa asks why أخت restores the omitted consonant in its plural but بنت does not, explaining this by analogy of each feminine plural to its masculine.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Usage can reverse the common pattern, and one poet uses both forms for rational mothers in a single couplet.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The poet's line witnesses the forms الأمهات and أماتكا being used for rational mothers.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The form أمهة is also attested, with an added ه followed by feminine تاء; a poem uses it.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Given the singular أمهة, أمهات may be its plural; the added ه also appears in هبلع and هجرع.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | بنات is the feminine plural of ابن; the source previously discussed its derivation and pattern at 2:40. | mentions 2:40
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farra says بنات is the plural of بنة with an open باء, with kasra signaling an omitted radical; the author says this works only if that radical is ياء, while the correct root is واو.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Another grammarian gives the original as بنوة; the author reconciles this with the بنة account, since both require the missing root letter to be واو.
[SAMIN-DURR:4:23/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The تاء in بنت and أخت compensates for an omitted root consonant rather than marking femininity: the preceding consonant is still, and the تاء does not become هاء in pause.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p247#2/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The verse prohibits marriage to relatives by blood, with further prohibitions through nursing and affinity.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p247#2/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas classifies seven prohibited relations by blood and seven by affinity.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p247#2/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · جمهور العلماء | reports | Most scholars prohibit a daughter conceived through fornication because the verse’s general ‘your daughters’ includes her; Abu Hanifa, Malik, and Ahmad hold this view.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p247#2/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · الشافعي | reports | A view attributed to al-Shafi‘i permits her because she is not a legally recognized daughter and, like a child outside the inheritance rule, does not inherit.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p248/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet taught that nursing prohibits the same relations as birth; Muslim also gives the wording that nursing prohibits what lineage prohibits.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p248/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | rejects | Reports that the nursing rule has four or six exceptions do not qualify the hadith: examples either exist through blood kinship or are prohibited by affinity.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p248/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · مالك | reports | Malik and others hold that

any nursing amount establishes prohibition, relying on the verse’s general wording; this is also attributed to Ibn Umar and early jurists.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p248/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · عائشة | reports | Another view requires at least three feeds, based on the Prophet’s statement that one or two sucks do not prohibit.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p248/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · أم الفضل | reports | Umm al-Fadl transmits a Prophetic report likewise ruling that one or two feeds or sucks do not establish prohibition.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p248/r6] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · عائشة | reports | A third view requires five feeds, based on Aisha’s report that ten known feeds were abrogated by five, which remained recited at the Prophet’s death.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p249#2/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | A wife’s mother becomes prohibited as soon as the marriage contract is made, whether or not the marriage is consummated.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p249#2/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | A stepdaughter becomes prohibited only after consummation with her mother; if the mother is divorced before consummation, her daughter may be married.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p249#2/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · بعضهم | reports | Some interpret the consummation condition as applying to both mothers and stepdaughters, so neither is prohibited before consummation with the other.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p249#2/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · علي | reports | Ali compares the wife’s mother to a stepdaughter in the case of a man who divorced before consummation, applying the entry condition to her too.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p249#2/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · زيد بن ثابت | reports | Zayd ibn Thabit says a man who divorces before consummation may marry his former wife’s mother.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p249#2/r6] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · زيد بن ثابت | reports | Zayd disliked marrying the mother if the wife died and the husband inherited from her, but allowed it after divorce before consummation.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p249#2/r7] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas permitted marrying the mother in a case where the man had not consummated the marriage to her daughter.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p249#2/r8] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عمر | reports | Ibn Umar forbade marrying the mother in that case.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p249#2/r9] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · معاوية | reports | Muawiya declined to declare what God permitted or prohibited and pointed out that many other women were available.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p249/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · سهلة بنت سهيل | reports | In the Salim case the Prophet ordered Sahla to nurse Abu Hudhayfa’s freedman five times; Aisha used five feeds for women seeking access, and al-Shafi‘i and his followers adopted this view.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p249/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · جمهور العلماء | reports | The majority require nursing to occur while the child is under two years old, linking the issue to 2:233. | mentions 2:233
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p249/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · جمهور الأئمة الأربعة | reports | The four Sunni schools and others hold that milk kinship extends through the nursing father as well as the nursing mother.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p249/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · بعض السلف | reports | Some early authorities restrict milk kinship to the nursing mother and do not extend it through the father.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p250/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · عبد الله بن الزبير | reports | Ibn al-Zubayr treats the stepdaughter and her mother alike: both are permissible if the man did not consummate the marriage with the woman.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p250/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid says the consummation condition applies to both the wife’s mother and her daughter.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p250/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Ibn Kathir says most early and later scholars reject that reading: a stepdaughter is prohibited only after consummation with her mother, while the mother is prohibited at contract.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p250/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas reportedly held that the wife’s mother remains prohibited if the wife dies or is divorced before consummation, calling her prohibition unrestricted.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p250/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Ibn Kathir identifies the view that a wife’s mother is prohibited by contract as the position of the four imams, seven jurists, and the majority across generations.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p251/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Although the cited Prophetic report has a problematic chain, Ibn Kathir says the established consensus makes separate authentication unnecessary.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p251/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | reports | The hadith also states that the Prophet’s stepdaughter was his niece through nursing, an additional bar to marriage.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p251/r3] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The stepdaughter is prohibited whether or not she was raised in the husband’s home; ‘in your care’ describes what is usual and carries no restrictive implication, as at 24:33. | mentions 24:33
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p251/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · أم حبيبة | reports | Umm Habiba asked the Prophet to marry her sister, and he answered that this was unlawful.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p251/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Ibn Kathir says the Prophet’s ruling makes marriage to the mother the basis for the stepdaughter’s prohibition; the girl was also his milk-niece.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p251/r6] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · بعضهم | reports | A minority view says a stepdaughter is prohibited only if she was raised in the man’s household.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v2p252/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The chain supporting Ali’s view that a stepdaughter outside the husband’s household is lawful is strong by Muslim’s standard, though Ibn Kathir calls the view very unusual.
