[ITQAN:v1p223/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | A sufficient stop is detached in wording but connected in meaning, allowing a pause and restart; “your mothers are forbidden” is such a stop.
[ITQAN:v1p223/r5] ITQAN, d. 911 · السجاوندي | reports | Al-Sajawandi classifies pauses into five ranks: necessary, unrestricted, permissible, permitted for a reason, and licensed by necessity.
[ITQAN:v1p229#3/r5] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Stopping after “your nieces” marks the transition from prohibitions by blood relation to prohibitions by marriage or other cause.
[ITQAN:v1p259/r7] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | When phonological and semantic causes coincide, Hamza fully lengthens for the stronger hamza cause and disregards the weaker semantic cause.
[ITQAN:v2p565/r2] ITQAN, d. 911 · ابن فارس | reports | Ibn Fāris and others distinguish ikhwa for brothers by lineage from ikhwan for friendship. | mentions 49:10, 24:31, 24:61
[ITQAN:v2p565/r3] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | reports | Suyūṭī notes exceptions to the plural distinction: believers are called ikhwa, while kin are called ikhwan in the verses on women's relatives and homes of brothers. | mentions 49:10, 24:31, 24:61
[ITQAN:v2p568#2/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Plural wording paired with plural wording can distribute to each individual: “your mothers” means each addressee’s own mother; likewise each has his own children and each mother nurses her own child. | mentions 4:11, 2:233
[ITQAN:v2p568#2/r3] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Sometimes plural-to-plural wording can support either distribution, so contextual evidence must determine which reading applies.
[ITQAN:v3p165/r6] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | The fourth deletion type, ikhtizal, covers omissions outside earlier types, including omitted nouns, verbs, particles, or multiple elements.
[ITQAN:v3p165/r7] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | A common omitted noun is the genitive complement: “your mothers are forbidden” means marriage to your mothers; Ibn Jinni estimates nearly a thousand such cases in the Qurʾan.
[ITQAN:v3p42/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · جلال الدين البلقيني | reports | Al-Bulqini calls a general wording that remains fully universal rare, since one can imagine a specification for almost every general text; he illustrates with several legal examples. | mentions 2:21, 2:173, 2:275
[ITQAN:v3p42/r3] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | The author limits al-Bulqini’s claim of rarity to subsidiary legal rulings and identifies the prohibition of close female relatives as a legal generality without exception.
[ITQAN:v3p42/r4] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | A general phrase intended specifically was never meant to cover every member; a specified general phrase was meant to cover them linguistically, though not all remain under its legal ruling.
[ITQAN:v3p42/r5] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | prefers | The first category is metaphorical by agreement; the second is disputed but the author prefers that it remains literal, as most Shafiʿis, many Hanafis, and all Hanbalis hold.
[ITQAN:v3p42/r6] ITQAN, d. 911 · أبو حامد | reports | Abu Hamid attributes the literal reading of the specified general to al-Shafiʿi and his followers; al-Subki approves because the word’s reach to the remainder is genuinely literal.
[ITQAN:v3p42/r7] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | The categories also differ in their indicators: the first has a rational indicator that cannot be separated, and may refer to one member by agreement; the second has a textual indicator that can disappear, and its singular reading is disputed.
[ITQAN:v3p43/r10] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Connected specification also occurs through a descriptive clause: the stepdaughters are specified as those in the husband’s household, from wives with whom he consummated marriage.
[ITQAN:v3p43/r8] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Examples of general wording intended to denote a particular are numerous, and the category exceeds abrogated passages because every general wording has some specification.
[ITQAN:v3p47/r3] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Although a praise passage might seem to permit combining two sisters through ownership, the non-praise prohibition against combining sisters limits that general reading. | mentions 23:5, 23:6
[ITQAN:v3p52/r5] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | reports | One view treats “your mothers are forbidden” as ambiguous because prohibition attaches to an act, not a person, and the omitted act could be supplied in several ways.
[ITQAN:v3p52/r6] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | reports | The opposing view says ordinary usage resolves the ellipsis: the prohibition means sexual enjoyment through intercourse or similar acts, as with other rulings attached to persons.
[ITQAN:v3p85#2/r6] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | prefers | The author regards these forms of implication as proof in principle, subject to conditions; most scholars reject an implication from stepdaughters being “in your houses” because that is the usual case.
[SUYUTI-TANASUQ:v1p71/r1] SUYUTI-TANASUQ, d. 911 · author | reports | An earlier argument is said to show that the present order of sūrahs in the muṣḥaf was established in the Prophet's lifetime.
[SUYUTI-TANASUQ:v1p71/r10] SUYUTI-TANASUQ, d. 911 · author | prefers | Suyūṭī prefers al-Bayhaqī's view that the order of every sūrah is divinely fixed except al-Anfāl and Barāʾah.
[SUYUTI-TANASUQ:v1p71/r11] SUYUTI-TANASUQ, d. 911 · author | holds | He cites the consecutive Ḥawāmīm and Alif Lām Rā groups, and the separation among the Musabbiḥāt, as signs of purposeful, divinely fixed sūrah order.
[SUYUTI-TANASUQ:v1p71/r12] SUYUTI-TANASUQ, d. 911 · author | holds | Placing Ṭā Sīn before al-Qaṣaṣ and separating it from the paired Ṭā Sīn Mīm sūrahs reflects their shared opening and relative length.
[SUYUTI-TANASUQ:v1p71/r13] SUYUTI-TANASUQ, d. 911 · author | holds | Al-Muṭaffifīn separates al-Infiṭār and al-Inshiqāq, although the latter two resemble each other in opening and subject and are longer than al-Muṭaffifīn.
[SUYUTI-TANASUQ:v1p71/r14] SUYUTI-TANASUQ, d. 911 · author | holds | He argues that without a divinely fixed order for wisdom, the Musabbiḥāt would be consecutive, Ṭā Sīn would follow al-Qaṣaṣ, and al-Muṭaffifīn would not separate the similar alif-lām-rā sūrahs.
[SUYUTI-TANASUQ:v1p71/r2] SUYUTI-TANASUQ, d. 911 · بعضهم | reports | Some cite letter-count patterns in the Ḥawāmīm and the sūrahs beginning Alif Lām Rā as a divinely grounded reason for sūrah order.
[SUYUTI-TANASUQ:v1p71/r3] SUYUTI-TANASUQ, d. 911 · بعضهم | reports | Some cite the semantic correspondence between a sūrah's ending and the next sūrah's opening, as with al-Fātiḥah's ending and al-Baqarah's beginning.
[SUYUTI-TANASUQ:v1p71/r4] SUYUTI-TANASUQ, d. 911 · بعضهم | reports | Some cite verbal rhythm or weight, exemplified by the ending of al-Masad and the opening of al-Ikhlāṣ, as a rationale for the order.
[SUYUTI-TANASUQ:v1p71/r5] SUYUTI-TANASUQ, d. 911 · بعضهم | reports | Some cite similarity between a passage in one sūrah and a passage in another, as in al-Ḍuḥā and al-Sharḥ.
[SUYUTI-TANASUQ:v1p71/r6] SUYUTI-TANASUQ, d. 911 · بعضهم | reports | Some say each sūrah's opening closely suits the previous sūrah's ending, though the relation is sometimes hidden and sometimes clear.
[SUYUTI-TANASUQ:v1p71/r7] SUYUTI-TANASUQ, d. 911 · ربيعة | reports | Ibn Abī Shayba reports that Rabiʿa was asked why al-Baqarah and Āl ʿImrān, both Medinan, preceded more than eighty earlier-revealed Meccan sūrahs; he answered that they were placed first through the compiler's knowledge, which the community shared, and this was not to be questioned.

[BURSEVI:v2p148#2/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | The majority hold that a wife's mother is forbidden whether or not the marriage was consummated; a Prophetic report allows marrying the daughter after divorce before consummation but forbids marrying the mother.
[BURSEVI:v2p148#2/r10] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The phrase حَلائل أبناءكم names sons' wives; حليلة is explained either by a wife's being lawful to her husband, living in his place, or each partner's access to the other's garment.
[BURSEVI:v2p148#2/r11] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The prohibition also covers women illicitly approached by one's son and comparable cases of touching or sexual contact.
[BURSEVI:v2p148#2/r12] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The phrase sons from your loins excludes adopted sons, while sons' descendants and milk sons, however far down, count as sons by lineage for this rule.
[BURSEVI:v2p148#2/r13] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | An adoptive father may marry the former wife of an adopted son; Muhammad married Zaynab after Zayd, whom he had adopted, divorced her, and critics were answered by revelation. | mentions 33:40, 33:4
[BURSEVI:v2p148#2/r14] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Combining two sisters in marriage is forbidden, while their simultaneous ownership is not; combining intercourse with both under ownership is included by implication because the operative basis is shared.
[BURSEVI:v2p148#2/r15] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The exception for past conduct is disconnected: past acts are not held against people; God forgives pre-Islamic conduct and is merciful to those who repent and obey.
[BURSEVI:v2p148#2/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · النبي عليه السلام | reports | The Prophet reportedly ruled that a man divorced before consummation may marry his former wife's daughter but may not marry her mother.
[BURSEVI:v2p148#2/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The rules also extend to women touched or otherwise sexually contacted, and mothers includes wet nurses and grandmothers.
[BURSEVI:v2p148#2/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | A rabiiba is a wife's daughter from another man, so named because a stepfather commonly raises her as he raises his own child; the term is an intensive form with passive sense, made into a noun by the feminine ending.
[BURSEVI:v2p148#2/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · ابن السكيت | reports | Ibn al-Sikkit says حجر has two pronunciations and denotes the cloth gathered over a person's thighs; in the verse, being in one's حجر means being raised in one's care.
[BURSEVI:v2p148#2/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The lap is a metaphor for upbringing because a caregiver seats a child there; it is comparable to being in someone's custody, from حضن, the armpit.
[BURSEVI:v2p148#2/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · جمهور العلماء | reports | The majority do not require a stepdaughter to have lived in her stepfather's care for the marriage prohibition to apply; the phrase reflects the usual situation, as wives with grown daughters rarely remarry while those with young children often do.
[BURSEVI:v2p148#2/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The same wording that reflects the usual case is compared with the prohibition of sexual relations during retreat in mosques, although relations outside mosques during retreat are also forbidden. | mentions 2:187
[BURSEVI:v2p148#2/r9] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Entering unto the wives means intercourse, expressed euphemistically as admission behind a curtain; touching and similar acts also count, and without intercourse a man may marry the daughters after separation or the mother's death.
[BURSEVI:v2p148/r1] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The prohibition of mothers means prohibition of marrying them, as customary usage understands a forbidden thing through its intended use: marrying women, drinking wine, and eating pork.
[BURSEVI:v2p148/r10] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The wet nurse’s husband is the nursling’s father and his parents are grandparents; his children by other women are paternal siblings, while the wet nurse’s mother and sister are grandmother and aunt.
[BURSEVI:v2p148/r11] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The wet nurse’s children by that husband are full siblings; her children by another husband are maternal siblings.
[BURSEVI:v2p148/r12] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet states the general rule that nursing forbids the same relations forbidden by lineage.
[BURSEVI:v2p148/r13] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Certain apparent milk relations are forbidden through affinity rather than lineage, including a father’s partner, a man’s partner’s daughter or mother, and a grandfather’s partner.
[BURSEVI:v2p148/r14] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Mothers of wives means women married to the men, whether or not the marriage was consummated.
[BURSEVI:v2p148/r2] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Mothers includes all ascending grandmothers through either parent; daughters includes biological daughters and all descendants; sisters includes full, paternal, and maternal sisters.
[BURSEVI:v2p148/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The bans on mothers and daughters have held from Adam to the present in every revealed religion; Zoroaster permitted them, but most Muslims judged him a liar.
[BURSEVI:v2p148/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | reports | A report says marriage between siblings was permitted in Adam's time only because of necessity.
[BURSEVI:v2p148/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · الإمام | reports | The Imam explains that intercourse is humiliating and usually hidden, so mothers must be protected from it because their benefaction is greatest; daughters are part of oneself and likewise must be spared this humiliation, as must the other listed relatives.
[BURSEVI:v2p148/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | A paternal aunt is any female child of one's father, near or distant; a maternal aunt is any female child of one's mother, likewise including sisters of ancestors through either side.
[BURSEVI:v2p148/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Nieces of brothers and sisters from every side, including their descendants however remote, are forbidden.
[BURSEVI:v2p148/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The verse names fourteen forbidden categories: seven by lineage and seven by cause, then begins the latter list with nursing mothers and milk sisters.
[BURSEVI:v2p148/r9] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Nursing mothers and milk sisters are forbidden like their counterparts by lineage; God gives the wet nurse the status of mother and a nursing partner the status of sister.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p249#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The prohibited women are prohibited as objects of marriage, not as persons: legal prohibition concerns acts, marriage is the salient intended act, and the surrounding context concerns marriage; therefore the verse is not ambiguous, contrary to al-Karkhī.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p249#2/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | The author regards the clause as performative rather than a report of a past prohibition; some investigators allow a report-like reading, taking the past form as timeless as in formal definitions.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p249#2/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The passive form is used because it is obvious that God is the one who made these women forbidden.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p249#2/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | “Your mothers” includes grandmothers at every level because “mother” denotes an origin, as in “Mother of the Book” and “Mother of Cities”; on this analysis the term's true sense includes them.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p249#2/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Some treat “mother” for a grandmother as figurative and establish the prohibition by consensus; the author says the intended meaning is “origin” either way, so grandmothers fall under the general figurative usage, with consensus identifying that intent.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p249#2/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Daughters include one's own daughter and descendants' daughters: “daughter” can truly mean a branch, or may be extended to descendants figuratively; even those who deny that extension accept their prohibition by consensus.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p249#2/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The prohibition of grandmothers and descendants' daughters can also follow from the text's indication: aunts are daughters of grandmothers, and descendants' daughters are closer than nieces, so the nearer relations are prohibited a fortiori.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p249#2/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The verse's apparent Arabic meaning prohibits marrying one's biological daughter born of fornication, since no evidence transfers the ordinary meaning of “daughter” to a technical legal meaning here.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p249#2/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shāfiʿī permits the fornication-born daughter to her biological father because lineage and its other legal consequences are not established for her, citing the Prophetic dictum that a child belongs to the marital bed.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p250#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو حنيفة | reports | In the school discussion of a concubine's child, Abū Ḥanīfa says that if the master did not withdraw and protected her from suspicion, religious duty obliges him to claim the child; withdrawal or failure to protect her creates a contrary presumption allowing denial.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p250#2/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو يوسف | reports | Abū Yūsuf says a master must claim a child born before he performed post-intercourse waiting, whether or not h

[ALUSI-FULL:v4p250#2/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعض فضلاء الدرس | reports | A scholar in the lesson argues that admission of intercourse aimed at procreation, or admission that the master did not withdraw and protected the woman, should establish lineage without requiring a separate statement “this is my son”; the author sees no obstacle to adopting this position in the school.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p250#2/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Al-Mabsūṭ says that a long delay supports assigning the child to the master because his conduct, such as accepting congratulations, indicates acknowledgment and functions like an explicit admission.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p250/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعض الشافعية | reports | Some Shāfiʿīs say the daughter becomes forbidden if the Prophet Jesus, at his descent, informs the man that she was conceived from his semen; the author replies that the Lawgiver severed her lineage from him, so her physical origin is irrelevant.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p250/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعضهم | reports | Opponents of the prohibition argue that biological paternity cannot suffice: a man who buys a virgin, deflowers her, and later fathers a child is not automatically assigned that child without acknowledgment; legal lineage cannot suffice either, since Muslim consensus denies the fornication-born child lineage from the fornicator.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p250/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | The author answers that biological fact makes a person the daughter of the man whose semen produced her, whether licitly or illicitly; physical part-wholeness is the basis of the marriage prohibition, and the mother is certainly forbidden her own child born of fornication.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p250/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | The distinction between a child separating bodily from its mother and a daughter separating from her father only mentally does not disprove shared substance; Arabic calls a child a piece of its father, and absence of inheritance from the father is due to consensus, not lack of true daughterhood.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p251/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · البحر | reports | Al-Baḥr distinguishes proof in court, which requires a claim, from the relation established before God, for which jurists do not require one.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p251/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The plural banāt is commonly derived from bint, whose lām is correctly said to be wāw; the deleted element returns in akhawāt but not in banāt, whose masculine is banūn.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p251/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الدنوشري | reports | A poem poses the morphological puzzle of why the plural of ukht restores its lost letter while the plural of bint does not, although both use a compensating tāʾ.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p251/r12] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | His proposed answer is that ukht carries a prefix connection suited to wāw, so it takes the lost letter back.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p251/r13] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو البقاء | reports | Abū al-Baqā argues that tāʾ in these forms is not feminine, since feminine tāʾ would follow a vowel and become hāʾ at pause; he analyzes banāt as banah.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p251/r14] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الفراء | reports | Al-Farrāʾ explains the kasra in banāt as a signal of an omitted letter; other grammarians take the original vowel as fatḥa, matching banūn, the Basran view.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p251/r15] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | In akhawāt the tāʾ replaces wāw, and the listed aunts include sisters across all three parental lines.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p251/r16] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Paternal and maternal aunts include descendants of grandparents at every generation, and this extension is agreed by consensus.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p251/r17] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الخانية والمحيط | reports | An aunt of an aunt is forbidden when the nearer aunt is paternal or both-sided, but not when she is maternal; the ruling follows whether the connection reaches a blood grandparent or only a grandfather's wife.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p251/r18] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · المحيط | reports | For an aunt of a maternal aunt, the aunt is forbidden when the nearer aunt is both-sided or maternal, but not when she is paternal, since the relevant link is a grandfather's wife.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p251/r19] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The same listed kinship prohibitions apply reciprocally to a woman marrying the corresponding male relatives.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p251/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | A child conceived from the master's semen is his child in reality; an illegitimate child is likewise, with acknowledgment strengthening the case.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p251/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Since the prohibition rests on filiation, real filiation makes marriage forbidden before God, even when inheritance and judicial attribution are not established.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p251/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | A fact may be true without judicial proof, and a judicial ruling may not match reality; he illustrates this with the Prophet's horse purchase and Khuzayma's testimony.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p251/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | One cannot conclusively deny conception from the husband in an east-west marriage, since extraordinary travel or a jinn could make intercourse possible.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p251/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الأصحاب | reports | The jurists deny a boy's paternity of a child born to his wife because intercourse is inconceivable; physical possibility is required, and marriage alone does not suffice.

[ALUSI-FULL:v4p259#3/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | If residence in the man's home mattered, the verse would have mentioned its absence as well; Arabic usage can attach negation of a ruling to the absence of the full or one part of its composite cause.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p259#3/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The phrase those from your loins is an adjective qualifying sons.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p259#3/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Ḥalāʾil means wives, named because spouses share a bed or go wherever the other goes; ḥalīl may derive from intimacy or from each being lawful to the other.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p259#3/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The verse directly forbids a son's wife; prohibiting other women the son has had intercourse with rests on separate evidence.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p259#3/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · إبن الهمام | reports | Ibn al-Humam says that if ḥalīla means bedmate or one whose clothing is shared, the term covers women possessed, approached by mistake, or approached through fornication, but not a merely contracted wife; other evidence establishes the son's fornicate as forbidden to the father.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p259#3/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The term sons includes descendants, so the rule forbids a descendant's wife to an ancestor, including a daughter's son.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p259#3/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · اللغويين | reports | Lexicographers apparently use ḥalīla for a wife; some instead choose the wider sense, including a slave woman, to include both wife and possession.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p259#3/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعضهم | reports | Some explain the broad term as warning that a man might assume his son's slave belongs to him because a child's property belongs to the father, and so might wrongly have intercourse with her.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p259#3/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Intercourse, not the mere categories of touching, follows the same rule as intercourse by sons.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p259#3/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The phrase from your loins qualifies sons and excludes an adopted son's wife; the verse was revealed after the Prophet married Zayd ibn Haritha's former wife, while the phrase does not exclude a nursing-son's wife, also forbidden.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p259/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Touching and similar acts fall under the textual indication of intercourse; the objection from the condition's contrary implication assumes a principle the author rejects, and any general implication could be specified.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p259/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Vaginal fornication creates affinity prohibitions according to the author, contrary to al-Shafiʿi, who says unlawful sex cannot create the prohibition that is a blessing; the author analogizes all intercourse to lawful intercourse because its capacity to cause offspring is the operative cause.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p259/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The author argues that lawful status is irrelevant: intercourse with a shared slave, a son's slave, a menstruating or otherwise prohibited partner, and other forbidden cases still creates the affinity prohibition.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p260#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · علي | reports | Ali reportedly said a man with two owned sisters who had intercourse with one must relinquish ownership before intercourse with the other.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p260#2/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The verse attaches prohibition to the act of combining, rather than permanently prohibiting the second sister, and the same principle covers combining a woman with her aunt or niece.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p260#2/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · النبي | reports | A report from al-Tabarani says the Prophet warned that combining relatives cuts kinship ties; a mursal report from Abu Dawud similarly gives fear of rupture as the reason for forbidding marriage over a relative.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p260#2/r12] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعض المحققين | reports | Some investigators treat the Prophet's express ban on marrying a woman alongside her aunt or niece as an interpretive explanation of the kinship rationale.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p260#2/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · علي | reports | Another report has Ali say one verse permits and another forbids the two owned sisters, so he neither commands, forbids, permits, nor prohibits the practice, and he and his household do not do it.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p260#2/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · إبن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas is reported to regard combining two owned sisters as permissible; the same view is attributed to Uthman.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p260#2/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · عمر | reports | Umar said he did not like to allow the combination and forbade the questioner from doing it.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p260#2/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعضهم | reports | Some say the Companions who initially allowed combining later adopted the majority view; if not, a later consensus overrides the earlier disagreement, and otherwise prohibition is preferred when reports conflict.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p260#2/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | A man may marry the sister of his owned slave with whom he had intercourse, but cannot have intercourse with either woman until he makes the slave forbidden to himself through sale, marriage, transfer, emancipation, or a similar cause.

[ALUSI-FULL:v4p260#2/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | If ownership of the slave returns by rescission or a new purchase, intercourse with either remains barred until the slave is again made forbidden to him; the school's wording implies the marriage is valid because it is contracted by a competent person upon a valid subject.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p260#2/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The objection that the wife is treated as sexually enjoyed by the marriage, causing a notional combination, is answered by the man's ability to end that status; actual intercourse is barred afterward, without invalidating the marriage.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p260/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The prohibition on combining sisters is coordinated with the preceding prohibited categories and concerns marriage, not merely ownership.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p260/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The rule covers sisters by blood or nursing; if a stranger woman breastfeeds two wives, their marriages are both dissolved.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p260/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الشافعي | reports | Al-Shafiʿi is reported to hold that, in that nursing-sister case, only the later marriage is dissolved.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p260/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Owning two sisters is not itself prohibited, but having intercourse with both is prohibited by textual implication because the same operative cause applies; this is the majority view, also held by Ibn Masʿud, Ibn Umar, and Ammar.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p261/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · آخرون | reports | Other scholars say the aunt-and-niece hadith is well known, authenticated or transmitted by major hadith collections, and accepted by early generations and many Companions; it can specify the general permission even if solitary.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p261/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · إبن الهمام | reports | Ibn al-Humam says fame must apparently be established because the hadith functions as abrogation, not specification.
[ALUSI-FULL:v4p261/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The phrase except what has passed is a disconnected exception; treating it as emphatic confirmation is inappropriate because the following description of God as forgiving and merciful does not fit emphatic prohibition.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p24/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Reports about occasions of revelation aid interpretation by clarifying intent, but they do not restrict a verse's wording to its occasion.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p24/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · تقي الدين السبكي | reports | Al-Subki says neither an occasion of revelation nor a specific discourse purpose restricts general wording; a specific statement followed by a general one does not narrow the general rule. | mentions 2:229
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p24/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Transmitted reports include the community's consensus on meanings, which must rest on evidence; examples include the maternal sister in the first inheritance passage and Friday prayer. | mentions 4:12, 62:9
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p24/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Some meanings are known necessarily: prayer denotes the prescribed ritual form rather than supplication, and zakat the specified wealth paid.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p77/r14] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Mecca had one count, and verse counts could differ among Kufan, Basran, and Syrian codices, which exegetes sometimes specify.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p77/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Verse lengths vary with rhetorical needs, including the placement of end rhymes in relation to preceding speech.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p293/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The passage moves from banning marriage to a father’s wife into listing prohibited relatives; the change from a future prohibition to ‘has been forbidden’ marks the latter as an established rule. | mentions 4:22

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p293/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | When prohibition attaches to the names of persons, it means prohibition of the usual act sought from them: eating carrion, drinking wine, and marrying mothers.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p295/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The Arabic names for family members are unusual because they preserve an older stage of the language, before later refinement.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p295/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas, as cited by Ibn Atiyya, said the listed women were forbidden in pre-Islamic Arabia except a father's wife and combining two sisters.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p295/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · محمد بن الحسن صاحب أبي حنيفة | reports | Al-Qurtubi transmits the same account from Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, who additionally confines the exception phrase to the father's wife and combining sisters.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p295/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | rejects | The claim that all these prohibitions were pre-Islamic cannot stand literally, since stepdaughters and foster sisters likely were not forbidden then.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p295/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | Islam instills reverence for close kin, removing them from erotic use even though marriage has a legitimate end and begins from desire.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p295/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The kinship prohibitions extend reverence from parents and children to nieces and aunts, serving the necessary preservation of honor and human refinement.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p295/r8] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | In “daughters of the brother and sister,” the definite article stands in for a possessive phrase meaning your brother and your sister.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v4p296/r7] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · عمر بن الخطاب، وابن مسعود، وابن عباس، والزهري، ومالك، والشافعي، وأحمد، والأوزاعي، والثوري، وأبو يوسف | reports | These authorities hold that nursing after the child has passed two years has no legal effect on kinship prohibitions.
